case_info.scenario: An 87-year-old woman was admitted due to sudden-onset worsening right facial swelling and pain persisting for 1 day. Additionally, she reported a decade-long history of a slow-growing cheek swelling. She denied any recent dental procedures, and there was no pain on mastication. On examination, she had a fever, and her right cheek exhibited gross swelling and erythema with mild induration. Intraorally, foul-smelling pus was observed with poor dental hygiene, as well as caries with pus expressed from the right second and third maxillary molars. Additionally, there was generalized maxillary alveolar hyperplasia noted, as depicted inFigure 1. She had full eye range of motion and no eye symptoms. Computed tomography (CT) results revealed a marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with a superimposed odontogenic and sinus infection?
case_info.caption: Clinical photographs showing generalized maxillary alveolar hyperplasia. The arrowhead depicts maxillary alveolar hypertrophy.
case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

dialogue_history.speaker: medical
dialogue_history.text: I disagree that Paget disease is the leading diagnosis here. The chronic maxillary expansion with mixed sclerotic-lytic areas and cortical erosions, combined with a superimposed acute odontogenic and sinus infection, is much more characteristic of a benign fibro-osseous lesion such as ossifying fibroma or fibrous dysplasia, not Paget's disease which typically involves the skull vault and pelvis. The immediate management priority remains addressing the acute infection with antibiotics and surgical drainage, but the underlying chronic lesion needs definitive biopsy and histopathological diagnosis.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.

   Definition:

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

   Definition:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: Figure 2depicts the CT of the face, which revealed marked expansion of the maxilla with mixed sclerotic lytic areas. There were areas of cortical erosions that were seen with diffuse soft tissue thickening with inflammatory stranding. Dehiscence of the right maxillary sinus floor with complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus was noted. She received a diagnosis of right sinusitis and facial cellulitis secondary to an odontogenic infection on a background of newly diagnosed Paget disease of the skull. She underwent an endoscopic drainage of the right maxillary sinusitis and dental extractions, as well as a course of intravenous antibiotics. She was discharged in good health and remained healthy at her follow-up review. Radionuclide bone scintigraphy performed showed increased tracer accumulation at the frontal, skull base, occipital, maxillary, and mandibular regions in the blood pool phase. In the delayed imaging, all these sites showed intense tracer uptake and appeared expanded. Paget disease, also known as osteitis deformans, is a chronic bone disorder characterized by the disruption of the usual cycle of bone remodeling that causes erratic bone resorption and formation. Various studies have suggested a potential connection between viruses, particularly paramyxoviruses and measles virus, and the disease’s pathogenesis; however, conclusive evidence is lacking.1There is a strong genetic component, and 15% to 20% of those affected have a first-degree relative with the disease.2Paget disease is most prevalent among elderly individuals and frequently observed in individuals older than 55 years. It exhibits a higher incidence in male individuals, with a sex ratio of 1.8:1. Geographical variations are notable; occurrence of the disease is rare in Asia, Scandinavia, and Africa.3 Paget disease exhibits diverse clinical presentations that primarily depend on the affected bones. Commonly involved areas include the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, skull, femur, or tibia. The condition can manifest locally in 1 or a few bones or extend widely throughout the skeleton, usually in the form of pain or increased bone size. Numerous authors have emphasized that bones affected by Paget disease are particularly prone to infection on exposure to oral flora.4This was apparent in this case, in which the patient presented with progressive cheek swelling with a superimposed dental infection. In some cases, Paget disease is asymptomatic and is incidentally discovered through radiological investigations or an increase in serum alkaline phosphatase activity. Diagnosis of Paget disease is primarily through radiological investigations. In relation to this case, there are classical features that may be seen on the skull radiography and CT. In the initial stage,Osteoporosis circumscriptamanifests as large and well-defined lytic lesions that involve the inner aspect of the outer table of the skull. The inner table remains preserved at this stage. The skull may exhibit a cotton wool appearance as the disease progresses. This refers to the presence of mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions that create a distinctive pattern on the skull. Advanced manifestation involves diploic widening in which the inner and outer calvarial tables are affected. A pathognomonic appearance associated with advanced Paget disease in the skull is termed theTam o’ Shanter sign, which is characterized by platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in the skull seeming to fall over the facial bones.5While radiological features are typically distinctive, occasional cases may make it difficult to distinguish between sclerotic or lytic metastases. For a thorough diagnostic evaluation, it is recommended to incorporate an isotope bone scan. This offers a comprehensive view of the entire skeleton, enabling precise assessment of the extent of the disease. The typical appearances on the scan, which are affected by skeletal metabolic activity reflected in tracer uptake, provide early insight into changes in disease activity.6 There are varied complications of Paget disease. Pagetic bone pain only occurs in a minority of patients. Deformities, such as femur or tibia bowing, may be asymptomatic or associated with mechanical pain. The predominant neurological complication in Paget disease is hearing impairment, typically originating from the affected petrous temporal bone. The deafness may exhibit conductive characteristics that result from middle-ear ossicle involvement, sensorineural features caused by compression of the auditory nerve, or cochlear engagement. Management of Paget disease centers around symptom control and reducing complications. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, play a crucial role in normalizing the aberrant bone remodeling process. Pain management and ensuring adequate calcium and vitamin D intake are integral components of the treatment approach.7 In essence, Paget disease presents a nuanced challenge in the realm of bone disorders. Management requires a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment to mitigate its effect on bone health and overall well-being.
